title: USE — resources (why is it slow?)
description: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — for every resource the service depends on. RED tells you the service is unhealthy; USE tells you which resource is the reason. Saturation (queueing) matters more than utilisation: a resource at 70% with a queue is in more trouble than one at 95% with none.

panels.title: CPU utilisation by container
panels.description: What the kernel actually gave each container. For a Node service, sustained CPU near 100% of one core means the event loop is the bottleneck — Node cannot use a second core for your request handler, so 'add CPU' does not help; you need to do less work or run more processes.

panels.title: Memory by container
panels.description: THE KEY PANEL FOR THE memLeak EXERCISE. Compare this against 'Node heap' below. In buffer mode this line climbs steadily toward the 512M limit while the heap graph stays perfectly flat — because Node Buffers live outside the V8 heap. One of those two metrics is lying, and this is the one that is not.

panels.title: NODE RUNTIME — saturation of the event loop
Event loop delay (p99) — the Node saturation metric
panels.description: How long a task waited before the event loop could run it. This is SATURATION, and for a Node service it is more diagnostic than CPU%. High delay with low CPU means you are blocked on something synchronous; high delay with high CPU means you are genuinely compute-bound. During cpuBurn this spikes hard while the DB and cache stay idle — that combination is the signature of 'the problem is us, not our dependencies'.

panels.title: V8 heap used (contrast with container memory)
panels.description: The metric most Node dashboards show — and the one that MISSES an off-heap leak entirely. Run `make leak-buffer` and watch this stay flat while container memory climbs. Then run `make leak-heap` and watch both move together. Same word, 'leak'; completely different visibility.

panels.title: POSTGRES — the resource everything else protects
Connection pool — in_use / idle / WAITING
panels.description: `waiting` is the most under-appreciated series in this lab. When it is above zero, requests are queueing for a database connection: nothing has failed, the DB is not busy, CPU is flat — and yet everything is slow. Pool saturation is invisible to both app metrics and DB metrics, which is why it is so consistently misdiagnosed.

panels.title: Postgres: rows fetched vs returned
panels.description: The N+1 detector at the database layer. Postgres reports no slow queries during an N+1 — each query is sub-millisecond and index-backed. What DOES change is the number of round trips. Watch tup_returned climb while query duration stays flat.

panels.title: Postgres: block reads (disk) vs hits (buffer cache)
panels.description: THE flushCache PANEL. When Redis empties, reads that were served from memory land here. blks_read climbing means Postgres is going to disk for data it used to have cached — the moment a *performance* component's failure becomes an *availability* problem.

panels.title: Postgres: active connections vs limit
panels.description: Utilisation of a hard-capped resource. Unlike CPU, hitting max_connections does not degrade — it REFUSES. Resources with hard limits fail cliff-edge rather than gradually, which is why they deserve their own alert.

panels.title: Redis keyspace hits vs misses
panels.description: Redis's own view, independent of the app's counter. Worth having both: the app metric only covers code paths you remembered to instrument, this one covers everything.

panels.title: Redis evictions — SILENT data loss
panels.description: Our Redis is capped at 128mb with allkeys-lru, so under memory pressure it quietly discards keys. Nothing errors. The app sees a cache miss and carries on. Evicted keys look identical to a cache that was never warm — which is why this counter deserves an alert even though nothing is 'broken'.

panels.title: Redis latency & clients
panels.description: Redis is single-threaded: one slow command blocks every other client. Connected-client count rising alongside latency usually means commands are queueing behind something expensive (a KEYS scan, a big pipeline, a flush).

panels.title: Outbound call latency (orders-api → payments-api)
panels.description: Client-side view of a dependency vs what that dependency actually spent. When THIS is slow but payments-api's own server-side duration is fast, the time is going into the network or your own connection pool — not into their code. When both are slow, it really is them. Trace-derived (spanmetrics), so the diamonds are exemplars: click one to open the offending trace.

panels.title: Database query duration (p99)
panels.description: From the app's perspective. Note during the nPlusOne exercise this stays FLAT — each of the 50 queries is fast. The damage is in the count, not the duration, which is precisely why metrics alone cannot find N+1 and a trace finds it instantly.
